fixes.explanation: Twelve years would be a short stretch, but the text says forty. Joash is the king of Judah, and the damage still hadn't been repaired by the twenty-third year of his reign (2 Kings 12:6). That's already almost double twelve.

Close, but the verse says something else. It says the high places were not removed, and the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there. So "visited" undersells it, because the people were sacrificing and burning incense at those places.

That's it. Joash tells the priests, "Collect all the money brought as sacred gifts into the house of the LORD…" He names the census money, the money from vows, and the money brought voluntarily. So this is money brought as sacred gifts for the house of the LORD.

No new tax appears anywhere in this passage. Joash points to all the money brought as sacred gifts into the house of the LORD. He names the census money, the money from vows, and the money brought voluntarily. A new tax from every town isn't on that list.
Right. Joash says, "…let it be used to repair any damage found in the temple." That's a money plan with no side quests, and I'd follow it any day.

Yes. Joash asks, "Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple?" By the twenty-third year of his reign the damage still hadn't been repaired (2 Kings 12:6). So he calls in Jehoiada and the other priests to ask. I'd want a very good answer ready for that one.

Yes. Joash says, "Now, therefore, take no more money from your constituency, but hand it over for the repair of the temple." The order has two parts. The priests are to take no more, and they are to hand it over for the repair of the temple.

Yes. Jehoiada set the chest "…beside the altar on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD." Jehoiada is the priest who took the chest and bored a hole in its lid. That puts it right where people come in.
No gate of Sur here. The text says Jehoiada set the chest beside the altar, on the right side as one enters the house of the LORD. That's where the priests who guarded the threshold put the money.

Right. When they saw a large amount of money in the chest, "…the royal scribe and the high priest would go up, count the money…" Then they tied it up in bags. The king's scribe and the high priest on one chest? I'd trust that pair with my cookie jar.

Yes. The text says the money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings "…was not brought into the house of the LORD; it belonged to the priests." So that money was not part of what came into the house of the LORD. The verse names the priests, so that's the word that fits the blank.

The poor aren't named here. The text says the money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into the house of the LORD, and that it belonged to the priests. So the money had a clear owner, and the text names the priests.

Gold is right. Joash sent Hazael "…all the gold found in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace…" He also sent the sacred objects dedicated by his fathers, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, the kings of Judah, plus his own consecrated items. That was a big load to send.

True. The text says, "So Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem." Hazael, king of Aram, had decided to attack, but he pulled back after Joash sent the gifts. Joash had sent him the sacred objects and gold before that.
Hezekiah isn't named in this passage. The text says Joash's son Amaziah reigned in his place. That's the name the verse gives, so it's the one that fits the blank.

Jehoram is one of the kings of Judah the text calls Joash's fathers (2 Kings 12:18), so he came before Joash. The son who reigned in his place was Amaziah. The verse names Amaziah as the one who took over after Joash.
